Section 5 • \(P\)3D

5.4 Reduction to \(\mu\) wedges, \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k)\rvert_{\mu\in(\mu_1,\mu_2)}\)

As for the 2PCF, both components of the wavevector must be expressed in the same units. Since \(k_\parallel\Delta=(\mathcal{J}k_\parallel)\,r_\parallel\), the comoving line-of-sight wavenumber is \(\mathcal{J}k_\parallel\), and we define \begin{equation} k\equiv\sqrt{k_\perp^2+\mathcal{J}^2k_\parallel^2}, \qquad \mu\equiv\frac{\mathcal{J}k_\parallel}{k}\in[-1,1], \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad k_\perp=k\sqrt{1-\mu^2}, \qquad k_\parallel=\frac{k\,\mu}{\mathcal{J}}, \tag{5.9} \end{equation} with the sign of \(\mu\) keeping the sign of \(k_\parallel\). The per-sample wedge is \begin{align} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k)\Big\rvert_{\mu\in(\mu_1,\mu_2)} &\equiv \frac{1}{2\pi\,(\mu_2-\mu_1)} \int_{\mu_1}^{\mu_2}\! d\mu \int_0^{2\pi}\! d\varphi_k\; \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}_{\perp}\!\left(k\sqrt{1-\mu^2},\varphi_k\right),\,\frac{k\mu}{\mathcal{J}}\right) \notag\\ &= \frac{1}{2\pi\,(\mu_2-\mu_1)} \int_{\mu_1}^{\mu_2}\! d\mu\; \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(k\sqrt{1-\mu^2},\,\frac{k\mu}{\mathcal{J}}\right), \tag{5.10} \end{align} and, for \(\mu\in(-1,1)\), the spherical average (monopole) \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k)\Big\rvert_{\mu\in(-1,1)} = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int\! d\Omega_k\;\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(\vec{k}\right) = \frac{1}{4\pi}\int_{-1}^{1}\! d\mu\; \mathrm{Re}\,\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}\!\left(k\sqrt{1-\mu^2},\,\frac{k\mu}{\mathcal{J}}\right), \tag{5.11} \end{equation} where the imaginary part drops because it is odd in \(\mu\) (Eq. (5.7)). For autocorrelations the wedges \((\mu_1,\mu_2)\) and \((-\mu_2,-\mu_1)\) coincide, and \(\mu\in(0,1)\) suffices.

Fourier link.

In comoving units \(d^2r_\perp\,d\Delta=\mathcal{J}\,d^3r\), so that, neglecting the window, \(\widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(\vec{k})=\mathcal{J}\int d^3r\;\widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(\vec{r})\,e^{+i\vec{k}\cdot\vec{r}}\). The angular average of the plane wave over the directions of \(\vec{k}\) is \(\frac{1}{4\pi}\int d\Omega_k\,e^{i\vec{k}\cdot\vec{r}}=j_0(kr)\), so the full-sphere wedges are related by \begin{equation} \widehat{P}_{ij}^{(s)}(k)\Big\rvert_{\mu\in(-1,1)} = 4\pi\mathcal{J}\int_0^\infty\! dr\,r^2\,j_0(kr)\; \widehat{\xi}_{ij}^{(s)}(r)\Big\rvert_{\mu\in(-1,1)}. \tag{5.12} \end{equation} This one-to-one correspondence holds only for the full sphere. More generally, expanding in Legendre polynomials, \(\xi(\vec{r})=\sum_\ell\xi_\ell(r)\mathcal{L}_\ell(\mu)\) and \(P(\vec{k})=\sum_\ell P_\ell(k)\mathcal{L}_\ell(\mu)\), each multipole maps onto the same multipole, \(P_\ell(k)=4\pi\mathcal{J}\,i^\ell\int dr\,r^2\,j_\ell(kr)\,\xi_\ell(r)\), whereas a narrow wedge contains all multipoles: the Fourier transform of a \(\xi\) wedge is not the \(P\) wedge over the same \(\mu\) range.
